summary: Mark Bissell presents mechanistic interpretability as reverse engineering neural networks to understand and manipulate internal representations. He references Anthropic's Golden Gate Claude demo, where neurons representing the Golden Gate Bridge were forced active, making Claude obsessed with the bridge regardless of topic. Bissell frames interpretability as moving from lab demos to practical value across three categories: developer tooling, UI/UX innovations, and frontier science. Drawing on his Palantir healthcare experience, he describes LLM deployment pain points: whack-a-mole prompt edits with off-target effects, costly LLM-as-judge setups, and fine-tuning problems like spurious correlations, mode collapse, and reward hacking. Goodfire's Ember platform addresses these via neuron-level debugging. He demonstrates attribution (inspecting which features fire for each token) and steering (amplifying a PII-sensitivity feature ~60% so a Llama model refuses to share a confidential email), plus dynamic prompting where a beverage feature firing triggers a Coca-Cola system prompt injection. Real-world users include Racketton for multilingual PII detection and Hayes Labs for red teaming guardrails. Model diffs, a research direction, enable git-diff-style comparison of feature changes during post-training, useful for detecting problems like sycophancy before deployment. Bissell then unveils Paint with Ember (paint.goodfire.ai), extending neural programming to image models: users paint concepts (pyramids, waves, lion faces) directly onto a canvas plugged into model neurons, with familiar tools like drag and erase. Features have adjustable strength and decompose into sub-features, enabling smooth interpolation between concepts (e.g., tiger equals lion minus mane). Additional use cases include explainable outputs for regulated industries, extracting scientific knowledge from superhuman genomics models (ARC Institute's EVO 2), novel biomarker discovery with a major health system, and efficiency gains through weight pruning. Bissell closes philosophically: engineers inherently want to understand systems, and the fact that we don't understand how models work is both frustrating and motivating. In Q&A, he identifies sparse autoencoders as the current best practice for finding features, with new methods expected.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction to Mechanistic Interpretability
sections.summary: Mark Bissell introduces himself and Goodfire AI, defining mechanistic interpretability as reverse engineering neural networks. He references Dario Amodei's piece on the urgency of interpretability and notes growing attention from major labs.

sections.title: Golden Gate Claude Example
sections.summary: Bissell explains Anthropic's Golden Gate Claude demo as a canonical interpretability example: neurons representing the Golden Gate Bridge were identified and forced always-active, producing a Claude variant obsessed with the bridge regardless of conversation topic.

sections.title: Three Categories of Interpretability Impact
sections.summary: Interpretability is moving from lab to real-world use. Bissell outlines three impact categories: developer power tools for neuron-level debugging, novel UI/UX interactions, and a long tail including frontier science in biology and genomics.

sections.title: LLM Reliability Challenges in Production
sections.summary: Drawing on his Palantir healthcare experience, Bissell describes familiar LLM development pain points: whack-a-mole prompt edits with off-target effects, costly LLM-as-judge setups, and fine-tuning problems including spurious correlations, mode collapse, and reward hacking. The common thread is a lack of rigor compared to traditional software development.

sections.title: Ember Platform: Attribution and Steering Demo
sections.summary: Bissell demonstrates Goodfire's Ember platform on a Llama chat model. He shows attribution by clicking a token to reveal internal features, then steers behavior by amplifying a PII/sensitive-information feature by ~60%, causing the model to refuse sharing a confidential email. He also mentions jailbreak resistance and conditional information lookup as other capabilities.

sections.title: Dynamic Prompting Demo
sections.summary: Bissell demonstrates dynamic prompting: a listener detects when a beverage/consumer-brands feature fires mid-generation and injects a Coca-Cola system prompt in real time, steering a generic drink recommendation toward Coca-Cola. The intervention is invisible to the user within a single real-time generation.

sections.title: Real-World Users and Model Diffs Preview
sections.summary: Bissell names real Ember users: Racketton for multilingual PII detection and Hayes Labs for red teaming guardrails. He previews model diffs, enabling git-diff-style comparison of feature changes during post-training, useful for detecting problems like sycophancy before deployment by observing which features and weights have changed most.

sections.title: Paint with Ember: Image Model Demo
sections.summary: Bissell unveils Paint with Ember at paint.goodfire.ai, extending neural programming to image models. Users paint concepts (pyramid, wave, lion face) onto a canvas plugged directly into model neurons, with familiar tools like drag and erase. Features have adjustable strength (e.g., turning up an opening-mouth feature makes a lion roar) and decompose into sub-features, enabling smooth interpolation between concepts—Bissell demonstrates that subtracting a mane from a lion yields a tiger-like image, suggesting the model internally represents tiger as lion minus mane.

sections.title: Additional Use Cases: Explainability, Science, Efficiency
sections.summary: Bissell outlines further use cases: explainable outputs for regulated industries like finance, healthcare, and law; extracting scientific knowledge from superhuman systems via partnerships with ARC Institute (EVO 2 genomics model, superhuman at predicting genomic data) and a major health system (identifying novel disease biomarkers, e.g., rheumatoid arthritis predictions); and efficiency gains through pruning unnecessary memorized weights to create specialized, lighter models.

sections.title: Philosophical Argument and Q&A
sections.summary: Bissell closes with a philosophical argument: the hallmark of an engineer is wanting to understand how systems work, yet we fundamentally don't understand how models operate—this alone justifies caring about interpretability. In Q&A, he identifies sparse autoencoders as the current best practice for finding features, while noting trade-offs and anticipating new techniques in coming years.

demonstrations: Golden Gate Claude demo (Anthropic): neurons representing the Golden Gate Bridge were forced active, making Claude obsessed with the bridge in all conversations
Ember attribution demo: clicking on the token 'confidential' in a Llama chat response revealed internal features like 'discussions of sensitive and protected information'
Ember steering demo: amplifying the PII/sensitive information feature by ~60% caused the model to refuse sharing a confidential email address
Dynamic prompting demo: detecting a beverage/consumer-brands feature firing mid-generation allowed injecting a Coca-Cola system prompt, steering the recommendation from generic cola to Coca-Cola
Paint with Ember demo: painting concepts (pyramid, wave, lion face) onto a canvas plugged into an image model's neurons, with drag/erase tools and adjustable feature strength
Paint with Ember sub-feature demo: decomposing a lion face into sub-features and interpolating to a tiger by subtracting the mane component, suggesting tiger equals lion minus mane
limitations: LLMs are non-deterministic, making precise behavioral guarantees difficult in mission-critical deployments
Prompt editing produces whack-a-mole off-target effects where fixing one issue breaks another
LLM-as-judge approaches are costly and introduce additional systems to monitor and maintain
Fine-tuning can produce spurious correlations, mode collapse, and reward hacking with unclear causes
Fine-tuning requires domain-specific data that is often difficult to curate
Sparse autoencoders, the current best practice for finding features, have trade-offs and may be superseded by new techniques
quantitativeClaims: Steering feature amplified by approximately 60% above normal level in the email confidentiality demo
Mark Bissell spent 3 years at Palantir working on healthcare initiatives before joining Goodfire
EVO 2 (ARC Institute) is described as superhuman at predicting human genomic information across organism types
